Teleport's documentation covers just-in-time (JIT) access to AWS roles through a few mechanisms. The key official pages are the role-request docs and the AWS integration guides.

- **Role Access Requests (core docs):** Users can request additional roles to temporarily elevate privileges, and requests can be routed through ChatOps or Teleport's Authorization Workflow API. Identity Governance is available only with Teleport Enterprise. The example role caps the session with a one-hour `max_session_ttl`.
- **AWS IAM Identity Center:** Teleport creates the account assignments only when a request is approved, and it removes them when the request expires. Assignments can also be made per Access Request, so a user can request specific permission sets for specific accounts. The AWS Account Assignments will exist for the lifetime of the Access Request, regardless of when the user assumes the associated role(s).
- **AWS IAM Roles Anywhere:** Teleport's role-based access controls and JIT Access Requests apply to console and CLI access. Credentials are issued only to authorized users, and for CLI and SDK based access, you must use tsh to obtain AWS credentials.
- **Role scoping:** Teleport roles can restrict which AWS roles a user may assume through `aws_role_arns`, and the docs say that field supports template variables populated at login.
- **Approval design:** Approvers are granted a role that lets them review requests for specific roles. In a worked example, a contractor requests a DBA role through `tsh login --request-roles`, and an approver reviews it with `tctl request approve`.

The search also returned some blog content with older examples and a 2021-era tutorial that uses outdated config versions, so check the current docs for exact syntax. The official docs are the more reliable source.

- **Plan policies** run after the plan succeeds and are the only policy type that can see the actual resource changes, so they're the place to enforce rules and automated review. Plan policies are the only ones with access to the actual changes to the managed resources. An example from the docs: a plan policy fails a run on a feature branch, but a repo admin can still merge if branch protection allows it.
- **Push policies** control what a Git event does. Pushes trigger runs by default. A push policy can start a tracked run (the apply path) once a PR is approved, mergeable, up to date with the target branch, and carries a `deploy` label, per the example in the docs. The docs define "approved" and "mergeable" differently for each VCS provider, so check your provider's section.
- **Approval policies** add human gates. Examples include requiring two reviewers on production stacks, which is distinct from PR approval. The FAQ notes that a run approval is a separate step from confirming the run, and nothing executes until someone confirms it.
- **Multiple policies of the same type** are evaluated independently and their decisions merged, so deny rules in one can block another's intent.

Caveat: the plan policy page in the results is marked as about 1,500 days old, so check the current docs for exact syntax and behavior.

The search didn't turn up a single doc page that covers all four pieces together, so the picture below is assembled from several Pulumi sources.

**Mandatory vs. advisory enforcement:** The CI/CD policy docs describe the behavior directly. An advisory violation logs a warning and the run continues, while a mandatory violation stops the operation and the pipeline (advisory violation logs a warning and the operation continues; mandatory violation fails the operation and stops the pipeline). Deployments inherits this: its runs execute the same commands, so mandatory violations fail the deployment and advisory ones show up in logs (policy packs in your stack's policy groups apply with no extra setup). One of the policy-as-code posts recommends starting new rollouts in advisory mode before moving to blocking (starting with advisory enforcement to gather feedback without blocking deployments).

**Pull request integration:** Pulumi's GitHub Action enforces policy packs automatically when a stack has them enabled (official GitHub Action that supports policy enforcement out of the box). For Deployments, the GitHub app gives PR previews so you can see changes before merging (full app integration with PR previews). Policy-as-code examples also show a PR-blocking pattern, though that is a generic CI example rather than a Deployments-native feature (policy validation on every pull request, blocking merges if violations are found).

## Research: change control and access patterns for an agent-assisted insurtech

Search-only research. I did not fetch full pages, so treat every item as a lead to verify. Several sources are vendor blogs, and some official pages were not returned at all.

**1. GitOps / PR as the only path to prod**
- **Core idea:** Plan on PR, apply only after approval and merge. Enforce policy as code at plan time.
- **Pulumi:** Deployments runs `pulumi preview` and `pulumi up` and applies stack policy packs. Mandatory violations fail the run. Advisory violations only log. The docs recommend testing in advisory mode first. [pulumi.com CI/CD policies](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/guides/policies-in-ci-cd/index.md). The CI/CD policy feature is listed for Team, Enterprise and Business Critical editions. [Pulumi drift/policy search](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/discovery-governance/policy/ci-cd/index.md)
- **Spacelift:** Plan policies are the only OPA type that sees the actual resource changes. Push policies can start an apply only when a PR is approved, mergeable and labelled. [Spacelift plan policy](https://docs.spacelift.io/concepts/policy/terraform-plan-policy), [Spacelift push policy](https://docs.spacelift.io/concepts/policy/push-policy)
- **Atlantis:** Plans on PR. Apply usually runs on an `atlantis apply` comment, gated by `apply_requirements`. OPA is a custom step, and the built-in integration is in Enterprise. Sources conflict on the default, so verify. [StackHarbor](https://stackharbor.com/en/knowledge-base/atlantis-terraform-pr-automation/)
- **GitHub controls:**
  - Rulesets and branch protection can require approvals, code-owner review, and "approval from someone other than the last pusher". [GitHub Docs: rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/available-rules-for-rulesets)
  - Environments can require reviewers and block self-review. The self-review option requires reviewers to exist first. [GitHub changelog, Oct 2023](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-10-16-actions-prevent-self-reviews-for-secure-deployments-across-actions-environments)
- **Pros:** Strong audit trail; the human approval is a named PR review.
- **Cons:** Only covers changes that go through git. Pulumi drift detection is detective and cannot block; the docs did not confirm whether drift findings can block a PR.

**2. JIT access brokers with Slack approval**
- **Teleport:** Role access requests can be approved in Slack. The AWS IAM Identity Center integration creates account assignments only for the approved window and removes them on expiry. Identity Governance requires Enterprise. [Teleport role requests](https://goteleport.com/docs/identity-governance/access-requests/role-requests/), [Teleport AWS Identity Center](https://goteleport.com/docs/identity-governance/integrations/aws-iam-identity-center/guide/)
- **Common Fate / Granted:** Requests come from the CLI, with auto-approval rules (for example, on-call status). Break-glass is off by default and enabled via Cedar. Slack approval is supported. The older Glide `granted-approvals` repo was archived in May 2024. [Granted access requests](https://docs.commonfate.io/granted/recipes/access-requests), [Breakglass](https://docs.commonfate.io/authz/breakglass)
- **AWS TEAM:** Approvals happen in its web app. Slack is notification-only in the sources found. Approve-in-Slack comes from community projects such as the FivexL `terraform-aws-sso-elevator`. [AWS samples TEAM](https://github.com/aws-samples/iam-identity-center-team)
- **Netflix ConsoleMe:** Self-service IAM requests with generated policies. A secondary source says the open-source version is being archived in March 2026 and has diverged from production. I could not confirm this on the primary repo. [github.com/Netflix/consoleme](https://Github.com/Netflix/consoleme)
- **Pros:** Time-boxed, auditable elevation with the approver named.
- **Cons:** Standing read access is still needed. Break-glass must be tightly logged and reviewed.

**3. AI coding agents and cloud access**
- **GitHub Copilot coding agent:** Runs in a sandboxed Actions environment with firewalled internet access and read-only repo access. It pushes only to `copilot/` branches. Workflows wait for a human to click "Approve and run". Extra scrutiny applies to `.github/workflows/`. Sources conflict on whether the requester's approval counts. [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/github-copilot-code-agent/2-security-risks-limitations-copilot-code-agent), [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/review-copilot-prs)
- **Claude Code GitHub Action on Bedrock:** Uses OIDC via `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`, `use_bedrock: "true"`, and `id-token: write`. Avoid `pull_request_target` with a PR-head checkout. [claude-code-action cloud providers](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/docs/cloud-providers.md), [Claude Code GitHub Actions guide](https://claudecode-lab.com/en/blog/claude-code-github-actions-advanced/)
- **Ephemeral, least-privilege sandboxes:** Use task-scoped, self-destructing environments, and keep live credentials outside the agent. A pattern treats agents as untrusted requesters that submit requests through a policy gate (MCP + OPA + ephemeral runners). [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/building-ai-agent-gateway-mcp). Netflix's Metaflow sandboxes are provisioned via Service Catalog and purged at expiry. [AWS blog](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/how-netflixs-ml-framework-metaflow-drives-open-source-adoption-with-aws-service-catalog)
- No Shopify, Stripe or Spotify first-party posts on this topic were found.

**4. Control mapping (partly unverified)**
- **ISO 27001:2022 A.8.32 (change management):** Requires change procedures for information systems, including impact assessment. Sources are consultancy blogs, not the standard text. [isms.online](https://www.isms.online/iso-27001/annex-a-2022/8-32-change-management-2022/)
- **A.8.2 (privileged access) and A.8.15 (logging):** Not verified. Search returned no text.
- **HIPAA 164.312:** Access control is (a) and audit controls is (b). Audit controls is a required standard. Verbatim text was not returned; check [eCFR 45 CFR 164.312](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-C/section-164.312). Source: [Bricker summary](https://www.bricker.com/insights/resources/key/hipaa-security-regulations-security-standards-for-the-protection-of-electronic-phi-technical-safeguards-164-312)
- **Mapping (my inference, not sourced):** PR review and environment approvals map to 8.32. JIT elevation maps to 8.2 and 164.312(a). Plan and apply logs with Slack approvals map to 8.15 and 164.312(b).

**Comparison**

| Approach | Speed for engineers | Compliance strength | Implementation effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| PR-only apply with branch rules and environment reviewers | Medium | High | Low |
| Pulumi Deployments or Spacelift with OPA plan policy | Medium-high | High | Medium |
| Atlantis with `apply_requirements` | High | Medium-high | Low-medium |
| JIT broker with Slack approval (Teleport, Common Fate) | High for access | High | Medium-high |
| Agent in CI via OIDC, approval-gated workflows | High | Medium-high | Medium |
| Agent sandbox accounts, ephemeral environments | Very high | Medium (depends on blast-radius limits) | High |

**Gaps:** No primary sources were fetched for Teleport, Spacelift or Pulumi pricing and edition details. The ConsoleMe archive claim and the Netflix production-access claim rest on secondary sources. ISO 8.2/8.15 and HIPAA verbatim text need the official standards.
